why: Each step needs 'the smallest remaining value, leftmost on ties' and then deletes a node and its current neighbours, which changes adjacency. A min-heap of (value, original index) gives the selection (original order equals current order among survivors), and a doubly linked list over indices (prev/next arrays) makes neighbour removal O(1); dead heap entries are skipped lazily.
hints: Two needs per step: find the minimum quickly, and find the current left and right neighbours after earlier removals.
Heap of (value, index) handles the minimum and the leftmost tie-break; prev/next arrays act as a doubly linked list so removing a task just relinks its neighbours.
Pop until you find an alive task, add its value, then unlink it and its prev/next neighbours, marking them dead. O(n log n).
pitfalls: Neighbours are in the CURRENT array: after removals, tasks that were far apart can become adjacent (example 2).
Ties go to the smallest index; (value, index) tuples in the heap do this for free.
Entries for removed tasks stay in the heap; check an alive flag before using a popped entry.
The first or last task has only one neighbour.
